title: About this site
text:
We believe in ‘predictions with zero BS’ and so that’s why we called this site ‘p0bs’.
And it is possible that we’ll predict other things in the future, but we’re happy to focus on the Premier League for now.
As with anything technical today, someone will ask about AI, so we’ll answer:

AI didn’t write any words here
However, we did use AI in a similar way to how we would have used StackOverflow in the past
AI was really useful at helping us to plan the architecture of this site and its associated calculations
Once validated (because it lied repeatedly), AI also helped to create a faster simulator for our code, using C++ (which we tested for correctness in the private R package that runs these calculations)
Although it wasn’t a linear process, AI also helped us with incremental improvements to the interactive charts and tables that reside in the aforementioned R package; the output of which forms part of this site

title: Our approach to calculating the numbers
text:
The fundamental purpose of this site is to predict the result of a future game in the Premier League. (After all, if we can do this for one game, we can do it for a whole season of games.)
To predict a game, we look across the past results of all the teams in the league. We then find the ideal mix of three settings that best matches these past results. These settings are:

The strength of each side
The importance of home advantage across all teams
The likelihood of a draw in an even contest

As it happens, using just these three settings proves to be a reliable way to predict the results from games in a new season. The same cannot always be said for approaches with more bells and whistles.

title: Our approach to calculating the numbers
text:
The fundamental purpose of this site is to predict the result of a future game in the Premier League. (After all, if we can do this for one game, we can do it for a whole season of games.)
To predict a game, we look across the past results of all the teams in the league. We then find the ideal mix of three settings that best matches these past results. These settings are:

The strength of each side
The importance of home advantage across all teams
The likelihood of a draw in an even contest

As it happens, using just these three settings proves to be a reliable way to predict the results from games in a new season. The same cannot always be said for approaches with more bells and whistles.

title: Our approach to calculating the numbers
text:
The detail
The idea to use these ‘three settings’ came from Davidson and Beaver (1977). In the notation of their paper below:

i is the home team and j is the away team
The bit on the left side of the first equation means ‘the probability of i beating j’ (i.e. the chance of a home win)
The second equation deals with an away win
The final equation shows the chance of a draw




If we add the numerator of all three equations, we get the denominator of each equation. This means that the probability of a home win, away win and draw rightly sum to 100%.
Looking in a bit more detail, we see these ‘three settings’:

\(\pi_i\) and \(\pi_j\) are the strengths (of the home and away sides, respectively)
\(\gamma\) is the home advantage (which is between 0 and 1, dampening the usual strength of the away side)
\(\nu\) is a parameter that deals with the likelihood of a draw in an even contest

This all seems complicated but the reality is simpler.
In short, our approach reduces to collecting the past results for all the teams in the league, before finding the ideal mix of the three settings that best matches these previous results. To find this ideal mix of settings, we use the implementation from the BradleyTerry2 package (2010).

title: Our approach to calculating the numbers
text:
A worked example
Let’s make our predictions for a specific game. In this case, we’ll choose a late-season game from a previous season, with Aston Villa at home to Tottenham Hotspur, and use the settings as they were then. (Of course, you could use the current settings, shown later on this page, should you wish.)
Going back to the snippet above, we now have:

\(\pi_i\) – the strength of Aston Villa (0.0615)
\(\pi_j\) – the strength of Tottenham Hotspur (0.0321)
\(\gamma\) – the home advantage shown across all grounds in the league (0.687)
\(\nu\) – a parameter that helps to determine the likelihood of a draw for an even contest (0.220)


Substituting these example settings into the three equations gives us our predictions for this game. Let’s start with a home win.
\[
P(VillaWins)
=
\frac{\pi_i}
     {\pi_i + \gamma \pi_j + \nu (\pi_i \pi_j)^{1/2}}
\]
In other words,
\[
P(VillaWins)
=
\frac{0.0615}
     {0.0615 + 0.0687*0.0321 + 0.220*(0.0615*0.0321)^{1/2}}
\]
… which becomes,
\[
P(VillaWins)
=
\frac{0.0615}
     {0.0735}
= 0.8370
\]

And now for the away win,
\[
P(TottenhamWins)
=
\frac{\gamma \pi_j}
     {\pi_i + \gamma \pi_j + \nu (\pi_i \pi_j)^{1/2}}
\]
That is:
\[
P(TottenhamWins)
=
\frac{0.0687*0.0321}
     {0.0735}
=
\frac{0.0022}
     {0.0735}
= 0.0300
\]

Finally, let’s consider the draw.
\[
P(Draw)
=
\frac{\nu (\pi_i \pi_j)^{1/2}}
     {\pi_i + \gamma \pi_j + \nu (\pi_i \pi_j)^{1/2}}
\]
That is,
\[
P(Draw)
=
\frac{0.220*(0.0615*0.0321)^{1/2}}
     {0.0735}
=
\frac{0.0098}
     {0.0735}
= 0.1330
\]

Bringing together these calculations, we get our predictions: an 83.7% chance of a home win for Aston Villa; a 3.0% chance of an away win for Tottenham Hotspur; and a 13.3% chance for a draw.

title: Our approach to calculating the numbers
text:
Our assumptions
In order to predict anything, you need to make assumptions. Some of these assumptions are explicit, whilst others are implicit.
To consider this statement further, let’s return to our example.
Over the last two full seasons, Tottenham Hotspur has struggled, finishing in 17th position on each occasion. Our predictions reflect that reality in assigning the team its relatively-weak strength setting.
However, our predictor doesn’t know that a highly-regarded new manager has been recently been hired, spending lots of money on new players.
Given this potential weak point in our approach, we often find it useful to blend the results from a longer-term assessment (over two and a bit years) with corresponding results from a shorter-term assessment (perhaps over the last half-season). In doing so, we boost the importance of more recent results in our predictions.
Furthermore, given that the model only considers results, it cannot directly reflect specific events, such as tragedies or points deductions (although ‘what-if’ analysis could be conducted for given levels of points deduction for a specific team).
Whilst this is not an exhaustive list of assumptions, the final one to note is that the team strengths are fixed across the year when they are set and are not assumed to evolve week-by-week based upon future performances.
Overall, this suggests that our model is useful in simplifying the real world in order to give a framework to understand the mechanisms at play in the Premier League competition. It is not, however, a way to predict with perfect foresight the outcome of any game or season. As such, if a number says 0% or 100%, treat it with a pinch of salt.

title: Using Charts to Show the Same Information
text:
On our home page, we saw a table that answered the following important questions. We now consider the same questions but answer them by using charts.


What are my team’s chances this season? And how important is their next game?

Each dot of this chart shows the outcome of a different scenario for where a team finishes in the league this season. The higher the dot, the better the finish.
With each team, there are four series:

The scenarios associated with the team’s prospects NOW (in grey)
What those prospects will become if the team’s players LOSE their next game (in red)
What those prospects will become if the team’s players DRAW their next game (in amber)
What those prospects will become if the team’s players WIN their next game (in green)

We order the teams according to their current expected position at the end of the season, denoted by the dark horizontal line (median) for the team’s series in grey.




We also note that:

You can hover over any scenario (i.e. dot) on the chart for further details about it
Whilst there are many dots on this plot, we actually generate far more scenarios than this in reality. We’ve merely summarised them on the chart for the sake of aesthetics
We have also created this non-interactive version of the chart
You might want to peruse our approach and its associated caveats, such as: the fact that values like 0% or 100% aren’t always quite what they seem; or our license about how to use (or not use) these values.

title: Premier Prediction
text:
Will my side win the title this season? Or are they going to be relegated?
On this site, we answer these questions about the Premier League. And you’re probably thinking, “but lots of sites answer these questions.”
And you’d be right. But unlike other prediction sites, we also focus on what will change if your team loses, draws or wins its next game. That way, you can answer another crucial question: How important is my team’s next game? That’s a question we often have, which is why we built this site the way that we did.


What are my team’s chances this season? And how important is their next game?

In each cell of the table below, the large number in bold is the current chance of a season-long event happening. Of Arsenal being the winner, for example, or of Liverpool finishing in the top 5. The small numbers below it show what that chance will become if the team loses, draws or wins its next game. Below each team’s name, you’ll also find its opponent in this next game.




As you’ll see, some games really don’t matter much. That is, the chances for some teams barely change due to the result of the next game. Consider the example where your team is near the top of the table after ten games, having made it into the Champions League in the previous season. In this case, the odds of your team finishing in the top five this year aren’t really going to change if your next game is away to the current champions (although your odds of being champions might).
Conversely, if your team is new to the league and sits mid-table after ten games then its next result likely matters a lot to its chances of finishing in the top half or getting relegated. (That’s because the model behind these calculations uses past results and doesn’t have much Premier League history for this team, making one more data point particularly insightful.)


Details, details

While some people prefer tables of numbers to understand outcomes, others prefer charts that show the same thing. If that’s your preference, use our interactive chart.
You might also be wondering about the methodology that we used to calculate the values above. If so, peruse our approach and its associated caveats, such as: the fact that values like 0% or 100% aren’t always quite what they seem; or our license about how to use (or not use) these values.
